title: Delegate terms expire by default, making continuation an affirmative act rather than incumbency
content:
A.6.1.1.1.3.1.3.4.3 appoints Delegates to "fixed six (6) month terms aligned to calendar half-years (January 1–June 30; July 1–December 31)," and A.6.1.1.1.3.1.3.5.5 supplies the default: absent a recorded re-approval, "the Delegate is automatically offboarded effective 00:00 UTC on the day after term end."

The direction of the default is the whole decision. Under the ordinary arrangement — serve until removed — inertia favours the incumbent and removing anyone requires someone to act, take a position, and absorb the friction. Here inertia removes, and *retention* is what requires an act. A delegate who has quietly stopped adding value simply lapses, with no confrontation and no one needing to make a case.

Aligning terms to calendar half-years rather than to individual start dates converts a stream of scattered renewal decisions into two scheduled review moments per year, which makes the cohort comparable and the review hard to forget.

The transition clause shows the mechanism being applied to itself: pre-existing Delegates are "deemed approved through June 30, 2026," with the framework explicitly waiving the January 1, 2026 checkpoint so nobody lapses on a technicality during changeover.

Read against the independence tension in this framework, the same default cuts the other way: a delegate facing an expiry they need the Foundation to reverse every six months is more dependent, not less.
description: Six-month terms are fixed to calendar half-years and lapse automatically at 00:00 UTC after term end unless a re-approval is recorded, so inaction removes rather than retains.
